title: Badr: the day
hookLine: about three hundred against a thousand, two young men of the Ansar in the row, and the Meccan leaders fall (Muslim; Bukhari)

cards: Morning, by the wells. In Sahih Muslim, Umar says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ looked across at the Meccan army, a thousand men, and then at his own companions, a little over three hundred.

He turned toward the qiblah and raised his hands. By the time the day ends, Meccan leaders who had set themselves against the new faith are among the dead, and a small band that expected to be crushed is still standing.

teach.h: TWO YOUNG MEN OF THE ANSAR.
teach.b: A very human report comes from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market.

In Sahih al-Bukhari he says he stood in the row and found two young men of the Ansar on either side of him, and he wished for stronger men at his sides. Then one nudged him and whispered: uncle, do you know Abu Jahl?
What do you want with him? I've heard he insults the Messenger of Allah, the young man said. Then the other nudged him and asked the very same thing.
When Abd al-Rahman pointed him out, both went straight for him and struck him down. Afterward each told the Prophet he had done it.

The Prophet looked at their two swords and said: both of you killed him. The two he had wished away were the two who went straight for him. Later, Surah Al Imran looks back on that day, and it doesn't flatter anyone.
In Pickthall's words: "Allah had already given you the victory at Badr, when ye were contemptible." Contemptible is a strong old word: small, weak, easy to look down on.
The verse goes on: so keep your duty to Allah, that you may be thankful.
Surah al-Anfal says something close: remember when you were few, counted weak in the land, afraid people would snatch you away, and He gave you refuge and strengthened you.
So these two verses tell Badr less as a triumph than as a rescue. The point isn't how strong they were. It's how small they were, and where the thanks should go.

how: Muslims retell Badr in sermons and sirah classes, and the Qur'an's own reminder of it in Surah Al Imran and Surah al-Anfal is recited in prayer like any other passage.

games.q: you're Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, standing in the row at Badr. a young man beside you whispers: uncle, do you know Abu Jahl? what do you do?
o: tell him to go back to the camp.
ask what he wants with him, then point him out.
games.why: he asked why, heard that the man insulted the Messenger of Allah, and pointed him out. both young men went straight for him.

practice: Bring back one time you were outnumbered, by bills, a deadline, a diagnosis, a room against you, and look to your right and your left in that memory: who stood beside you that you didn't expect much from?
If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, for the rescue; if you don't, just hold that person in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Badr: the wells where a little over three hundred met a thousand, and the place the Qur'an names when it reminds the Muslims they were once small, and rescued. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the place, with its wells, where the battle was fought; the Qur'an names it in 3:123.

carryVoice: Your line: few against many. A week that began with a kneeling camel ends at the wells. Day seven hundred seventy-seven, done.
